flows_exercised: plain run x32 (core loop, two bursts of 12 and 20)

boredom_findings.what_gets_stale: The content, in two layers. Layer one: the corpus is 50 entries and the first exact repeat landed at use 12 ('Errors are values. - Rob Pike' at run 1 and run 12); across a second burst of 20, 'Plan to throw one away' came up twice and four quotes from burst one reappeared. A .bashrc user (the README's own pitch) has seen the pool's whole texture inside two weeks. Layer two, the deeper one: every quote is maximum-canon - 'Premature optimization is the root of all evil', 'Given enough eyeballs', 'billion-dollar mistake', Conway's law. For the programmer audience this targets, these are recognition, not discovery; by the tenth draw the dominant reading experience is 'yes, I know this one' rather than a small jolt. The interaction is a fortune(6) done right - quiet, pipeable, the em-dash attribution line is genuinely tasteful - so what wears out is strictly the pool, not the shape.
boredom_findings.suggestion: Out of scope this run (non-goal: corpus expansion), but must be named for the next one: the corpus needs depth from the second shelf - less-anthologized lines from the same canonical voices, and quotes from the last 15 years - plus some recent-repeat avoidance (a tiny statefile of the last N picks) so consecutive shells don't hand back the same greatest hit. The daily --seed pattern partially masks this and is the product's best idea; lean into it.
boredom_findings._conductor_verdict: REPRODUCED and STRENGTHENED. Gate check C4/C8: corpus is 50 entries; under uniform draws the MEDIAN first exact repeat is draw 9 and P(repeat by draw 12) = 76.2%. The agent's use-12 observation is therefore CONSERVATIVE, not a lucky anecdote. Severity 'notable' accepted after review, not rubber-stamped - the product's shape held across 32 runs; only the pool ran out. Filed as TS-1 (blocked on a human scope decision).

boredom_findings.what_gets_stale: Small tag pools exhaust almost instantly. --list --tag philosophy shows the entire pool is 3 quotes (two of them Dijkstra); after three filtered draws there is literally nothing left to discover in that tag, and the 3-4-count tags (philosophy, language, process, readability, reliability) all hit this wall within a session. The README's boast that 'the smallest pool holds three aphorisms, so --tag always has something to choose between' is technically true and experientially thin - three is a foregone conclusion by the third use.
boredom_findings.suggestion: Same root cause as the corpus finding: the thin tags need entries, not code. Until then the docs could steer users toward the 5+ pools as the tags worth filtering on.
boredom_findings._conductor_verdict: REPRODUCED EXACTLY. Gate check C6: philosophy=3 (two Dijkstra, one Alan Kay), and exactly the five named tags (language, philosophy, process, readability, reliability) hold <= 4 entries, 5 of 12. Filed as TS-2 (blocked, same scope lock).

boredom_findings.where: random draws across a session (voice distribution)
boredom_findings.what_gets_stale: Author skew: NDJSON analysis shows 24 authors but Dijkstra holds 7 of 50 entries and Perlis/Pike 5 each - a third of the corpus is three voices. Across 32 runs the Dijkstra-adjacent aphorism register (austere, epigrammatic, mid-century) recurs enough that draws start sounding same-voiced even when the words differ.
boredom_findings.suggestion: When the corpus expands, diversify voice and era before adding more Dijkstra.
boredom_findings._conductor_verdict: REPRODUCED EXACTLY. Gate check C4/C5: 24 distinct authors; Dijkstra 7 + Perlis 5 + Pike 5 = 17/50 = 34%. Filed as TS-3 (blocked, same scope lock).

boredom_findings.what_gets_stale: The second-session question 'what tags can I filter on?' has no first-class answer. Help says: Run --list --json | jq '.tags[]' to see tags - which is not pasteable as printed (no binary name, and .tags[] on NDJSON needs jq -s or dedup to be useful) and outsources basic vocabulary discovery to jq or to reading README tables. New flags are a non-goal so --tags is off the table this run, but the help text could at least print a copy-pasteable full command.
boredom_findings.suggestion: Make the help snippet a complete, runnable command line; note --tags as a candidate for a future run.
